inline.s: Bobang diyu (the hell of flaying): as for a person who slaughters cattle and snakes.
Yinxue diyu (the hell of drinking blood): the blood of the offender is drunk.
Shaoshou diyu (the hell of burning hands): the offender's hands are burned.
Shaojiao diyu (the hell of burning feet): the offender's feet are burned.
Daoci diyu (the hell of reversed barbs): iron barbs pierce upward into the offender, hooking his flesh backward.
Huowu diyu (the hell of the fire house): the house is made of hot iron, its flames blazing.
Tiewu diyu (the hell of the iron house): its name differs slightly from the fire house, but the meaning is the same.
Huolang diyu (the hell of fire wolves): fire wolves devour the offenders.
Yegan rushi (such is the retribution of karma): the painful retributions of the hells described above are all the fruits that sentient beings of Jambudvipa encounter by doing great evil karma.
Neng di Xumi (able to rival Mount Sumeru): the power of karma is so great that it outweighs Mount Sumeru.
Neng shen juhai (able to deepen the great ocean): the power of karma is deeper and broader than the sea.
Neng zhang shengdao (able to obstruct the holy path): such is the great power of karma that it blocks the practice of the transcendental holy path, so one cannot perfectly fulfil one's learning.
Xianhao shou zhi (even a hair's breadth must be received): however small the evil, like a hair, one must still receive its retribution.
Yecha shi zhi (the yaksha eats it): the yaksha (a man-eating ghost) eats the offender's heart.
Huotang sheng fei (the cauldron of soup boils fiercely): the hell of the oil cauldron boils the offender's body. 'Sheng' means fierce, raging.
Chen ji zuiren (rushing upon the offender): 'chen' means to chase, to pursue.
Yixiang hanbing (unbroken icy cold): the hell of ice and cold.

Chun fei jili (flying caltrops): 'jili' were weapons made of iron like spiked balls, used in ancient warfare. This hell is filled with red-hot iron spiked balls that fly back and forth, striking and piercing the offenders.

Wufei shi tong, shi tie, shi shi, shi huo (it is none other than copper, iron, stone, and fire): because when sentient beings do evil, their anger is like fire and their minds like iron and stone, utterly cruel with not a trace of softness, so their instruments of punishment likewise are none other than copper, iron, stone, and fire.
The Buddha emitted light and a great voice praising the Bodhisattva Ksitigarbha. The Bodhisattva Puguang asked about the benefits, and the Buddha explained them at length.
Fei ren (non-humans): refers to the ghosts and spirits among the eight classes of devas and nagas that resemble humans but are not human.
Miedu (extinction): that is, nirvana, also called entering extinction.
Dingshou (receive upon the head): expresses the utmost reverence, bearing the teaching upon the crown of one's head.
Diting (listen attentively): to listen with careful attention.
Weiran (so be it): to assent respectfully: yes.
Zengcai (colored silk): 'zeng' (read zeng), a general term for silk textiles; zengcai means colored silk, used to make offerings to the Buddhas and bodhisattvas and to adorn the place of practice.
Chuangfan (banners and streamers): flags used to adorn the Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and the place of practice; the cylindrical ones are chuang (banners), and the long streamers are fan.
Shiqing zhi jian (within the time of a meal): the time it takes to eat a single meal.

Zuo zhu jiyue (making various kinds of music): playing various kinds of sublime music that brings forth joy and a pure mind in people, such as Sanskrit hymns and Dharma music, nurturing the thought of the Way and guiding people to give rise to faith, and with beautiful melodies praising the supreme virtue of the great being; not ordinary worldly music. 'Ji' (read ji) generally refers to song and dance performance.

He kuang qin shou zhu heng (how much less to suffer calamities in person): that is, one does not meet with sudden calamities and disasters. Those who cultivate the Dharma-gate of Ksitigarbha can obtain the protection of hundreds and thousands of ghosts and spirits, so that whether in this life or the next they can dissolve calamities and avert misfortune.

Wang sheng ji hui (rashly generating ridicule and slander): recklessly spreading rumors, mocking and defaming, denying the benefits of the cultivators' merit, and destroying others' aspiration for the Way.
Huo lu chi xiao (or baring the teeth in laughter): or laughing wildly without restraint.

Xian jie (the auspicious aeon): the present great aeon. Because in this aeon a thousand Buddhas appear in the world, it is called the auspicious aeon, also called the good aeon. Our teacher Shakyamuni Buddha is the fourth Buddha among the thousand Buddhas of the auspicious aeon.
Egui (hungry ghosts): these ghosts have throats as thin as needles, bellies as large as drums, and flames of hunger issuing from their mouths.

Zhu gen bu ju (imperfect faculties): 'the faculties' refers to the six faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. 'Imperfect faculties' refers to being crippled, idiotic, insane, and the like.
Jiu chu chuang zhen (long abiding on bed and pillow): to be long bedridden with illness.

Huo you xian dao, huo duo yanmei, gong guishen you (or wandering in dangerous paths, or often haunted in slumber, roaming with ghosts and spirits): often having nightmares, or dreaming of evil ghosts at night, or dreaming of deceased relatives and friends, or dreaming of wandering in evil realms, or dreaming of walking mountain paths fraught with danger, or being pressed down by a night-mare ghost and unable to move, or dreaming of roaming together with ghosts and spirits. 'Yan' is read 'an.'
Wangzhai (wasting illness): 'wang' (read wang) means extremely weak; 'zhai' (read zhai) means internal and external injury, often referring to consumption.

Yedao lundui (debate and confrontation in the karmic paths): these all arise from the accumulated evil karma of past lives, and at the time of death, in the realm of karma or before King Yama, one's enemies and creditors argue and confront one.
Wei ding qingzhong (not yet determined light or heavy): the offense has not yet been judged.
Mou jia (so-and-so): a pronoun of self-reference.

San bai bing ren (to speak it three times to the patient): to say it three times so that the patient hears and gives rise to a joyful heart, thereby disentangling his grievances and releasing his offenses.
Chali (kshatriya): the royal and warrior class of India.

Yu yue yiri ... naizhi sanshi ri (on the first of the month ... up to the thirtieth): according to the lunar calendar, in a large month the days are the first, eighth, fourteenth, fifteenth, eighteenth, twenty-third, twenty-fourth, twenty-eighth, twenty-ninth, and thirtieth. In a small month they are the first, eighth, fourteenth, fifteenth, eighteenth, twenty-third, twenty-fourth, twenty-seventh, twenty-eighth, and twenty-ninth.
Neng yu shi zhai ri, mei zhuan yibian (to be able, on each of the ten fasting days, to recite it once): on every one of the ten fasting days, recite the Ksitigarbha Sutra once.
Ji (verse): 'ji' (read ji), an abbreviation of the Sanskrit 'gatha,' translated into Chinese as 'song of praise,' is a kind of rhymed text somewhat like poetry, usually four lines forming one verse.

Hugui (the barbarian kneel): an Indian custom of kneeling on one knee. The Chinese called the peoples of the western borderlands 'Hu' (barbarians), and their way of kneeling was called 'hugui.' The Chinese kneel on both knees, called 'chang gui' (the long kneel).
Weiran dingshou (so be it; I receive upon my head): I shall receive and practise it with the utmost reverence.

blocks.text: Chapter Seven: The Benefits for the Living and the Dead

inline.s: The Bodhisattva Ksitigarbha addressed the Buddha, universally urging sentient beings to cut off evil and cultivate goodness. The elder Great Eloquence asked about the merit of aiding the deceased, and the Bodhisattva explained to him that of seven parts, one is obtained.
Tuohuo shanli (to obtain the benefit of release): the word 'tuo'
here means 'if' or 'should'; one may happen to have the opportunity to cultivate goodness.

Ru lv ni tu, fu yu zhong shi (like treading a muddy road while bearing a heavy stone): the muddy road is a metaphor for the five turbidities, and the heavy stone for the evil karma one has created. Sentient beings, with heavy karma, are born in the five turbidities, and without knowing how to cultivate, they create further evil karma and sink ever deeper into delusion, unable to escape.

Ruo de yu zhishi, ti yu jian fu, huo quan yu fu: the good friend is a metaphor for the great being (a common term for a bodhisattva), and urging one to cultivate, acting as a powerful supporting condition, is 'bearing the load for one.' Helping one along to level ground is a metaphor for guiding one to cultivate goodness and bring about birth among humans and gods, and even escape the three realms; once born among humans and gods, the bodhisattva advises one to reflect and not do evil again. 'Shi zhishi' means 'this good friend.' Here the word 'shi' means 'this' or 'this one.'

Fumu juanshu yi wei she fu, yi zi qian lu (parents and relatives should make blessings to aid the road ahead): for sentient beings of evil habits, at the time of death, parents and relatives should create blessings to help them on the dark road, so that they do not fall. 'Zi' means to supply, to help.

Shi zhu zhongsheng suo zao eyi, ji qi gan guo, bi duo equ; yuan shi juanshu wei linzhong ren xiu ci shengyin, rushi zhong zui, xi jie xiaomie: these sentient beings, reckoning the evil karma they have created, must surely be reborn in evil destinies to suffer; but because their relatives cultivate this holy cause for the dying person and dedicate the merit of offerings, prostrations, recitation of the Buddha's name, and reading of the sutras, all those offenses are entirely eliminated and they do not fall into evil destinies.
Wangliang (demons of woods and water): wang are the ghosts of trees and stones and the mountain spirits, and liang are the monsters attached to the waters. 'Wangliang' is read 'wang liang.'

Jiashi laishi huo xiansheng, de huo shengfen, sheng ren tian zhong, yuan shi linzhong bei zhu juanshu, zao shi eyin, yi ling shi mingzhong ren yanglei duibian, wan sheng shan chu: if in a future life or in the present life the deceased obtained a sage's portion and gained birth among humans or gods, yet because at death his relatives created this evil cause by killing, it causes the deceased to be implicated in a confrontation with the harmed, and he is delayed from being born in a good place, and even the good place he attains is not outstanding. 'Sheng' refers to one who has attained outstanding accomplishment, such as a master hand, a chess master. 'Shengfen' means obtaining excellent accomplishment.
Jueliang san ri (three days without grain): a metaphor for having no merit and virtue.
Suo fudan wu, qiang guo bai jin (the burden carried exceeds a hundred catties): a metaphor for the heaviness of one's own evil karma.
Lin ren (the neighbor): a metaphor for one's six kinds of relatives.

Yi mao yi di, yi sha yi chen (a hair, a drop, a grain of sand, a mote of dust): a single hair, a single drop of water, a single grain of fine sand, a mote of dust. 'Di' (the classical character) is an old character, the same as 'di' (the standard character).

Huizhong you yi zhangzhe, ming yue Dabian: in the assembly there was an elder named Great Eloquence. This elder had long realized the unborn, and transforming and saving beings in the ten directions, he manifested in the body of an elder. 'Wusheng' (unborn) means neither arising nor ceasing, that is, the principle of nirvana.

Yi shi zhi gu, weilai xianzai shan nan nv deng, wen jian zixiu, fen fen ji huo: this passage should be kept firmly in mind. Upon hearing the Dharma, while the body is healthy, one should cultivate at once, for now a part cultivated is a part gained; what one cultivates oneself one obtains oneself, without looking to later generations.
Wuchang (impermanence): impermanence is another name for death; human life is impermanent in the space of a breath.
Mingming youshen (the wandering spirit in the dark): after death, the wandering soul in the netherworld (the intermediate body).
Qi qi ri nei, ru chi ru long (within the seven-seven days, as if demented and deaf): during the forty-nine days, the intermediate body is as if foolish and deaf, suffering exceedingly.

Huo zai zhu si, bianlun yeguo, shending zhi hou, ju ye shousheng (or in the various courts, arguing the results of karma, and after it is determined, reborn according to karma): 'zhu si' refers to the court of King Yama. Or at the court of King Yama one argues about the karmic causes created and what retribution should be received; after it is determined, one is reborn according to the karma created.
Wei ce zhi jian, qianwan chouku (before the verdict, a myriad sorrows): before the judgement is rendered, the intermediate body is overwhelmed with sorrow and suffering, not knowing where to go.

Shi mingzhong ren, wei de shousheng, zai qi qi ri nei, nian nian zhi jian, wang zhu gurou juanshu, yu zao fu li jiuba. Guo shi ri hou, sui ye shou bao: within the forty-nine days, the deceased, not yet reborn, hopes at every moment that his relatives will create the power of merit to rescue him. After that period, his offenses being established, he is born and receives retribution according to the good and evil karma he has done.

Yanfu zhongsheng, ruo neng wei qi fumu naizhi juanshu, mingzhong zhi hou, shezhai gongyang, zhixin qinken: sentient beings of Jambudvipa, if for their parents and other relatives after death they establish a vegetarian feast and make offerings with sincere and diligent hearts, such people benefit both the living and the dead. (Master Yinguang urged that, in the event of a funeral in the family, it is even better to lead the relatives to recite the Buddha's name; the benefit is greater!)

blocks.text: Chapter Eight: The Praise of King Yama and His Multitude

inline.s: The ghost kings and King Yama, relying on the spiritual power of the Buddha and the bodhisattvas, all went to Trayastrimsa and asked why sentient beings do not follow the good path; the Buddha explained with the analogy of a lost traveler. Then the evil-venomous ghost king and the lord-of-life ghost king each made good vows, and the Buddha praised and confirmed them, and bestowed upon the lord-of-life the prediction of the Way.

Yanluo (Yama): Sanskrit yama, translated into Chinese as 'binder,' having the meaning of a spiritual power able to bind and arrest offenders. Yama the heavenly prince is King Yama, who possesses heavenly blessings, with a position equal to the lord of Trayastrimsa.
Yi (to go to): the meaning of going to a place, specifically going to an elder or superior. 'Yi' is read 'yi.'

Nan Yanfuti zhongsheng, qi xing gangqiang, nan tiao nan fu: the sentient beings of the southern Jambudvipa have natures that are hard and obstinate, difficult to tame and difficult to subdue. The sentient beings of the southern Jambudvipa, when suffering, know regret, but once they have left an evil they forget it, and are not easily led.

Shi da pusa, yu baiqian jie, toutou jiuba rushi zhongsheng, zao ling jietuo: this bodhisattva, taking no respite from hardship, guides them one by one, hoping that the hard-natured sentient beings may quickly gain liberation.

Zi shi Yanfu zhongsheng jie e xi zhong, xuan chu xuan ru: the sentient beings of Jambudvipa have deep and heavy habitual karmic ties, unwilling to seek true escape. Occasionally they do a little of the merit of humans and gods, but once that merit is exhausted they fall again. Master Xing'an's Essay on Rousing the Bodhi Mind says: 'In the morning one leaves the dark gate, at evening returns; from the iron cave one departs for a while, and enters once more.' The hells last long, and the human realm is short, so one leaves in the morning and returns at evening, departs briefly and enters again.

Lao si pusa jiu jing jieshu er zuo dutuo: it toils this bodhisattva through many aeons, rushing about, to make sentient beings aware and to rouse their minds to cultivate; but alas the sentient beings do not awaken, and there is nothing to be done, so to this day he remains weary and unremitting, without rest.

Piru youren mishen ben jia, wu ru xian dao: for example, a man, having lost his own home, mistakes his way onto a dangerous path. This is a metaphor for sentient beings whose beginningless single thought of delusion stirs them up, giving rise to confusion and creating karma, and losing their original nature.

Rushi miren, zai xian dao zhong, xuyu zhi jian, ji zao zhu du: this lost man, on the dangerous path, in an instant is attacked by many poisons. Sentient beings, being deluded and chasing after states, create all kinds of evil karma as if poisoned.

You yi zhishi, duo jie dashi, shan jin shi du, naiji yecha zhu edeng: there is a good friend who understands many great arts and can subdue these poisons, as well as the yakshas and all such evil harms. This is a metaphor for the Bodhisattva Ksitigarbha, broadly versed in the Buddha's Dharma, with great spiritual power, who can guide sentient beings in cultivating, be a powerful supporting condition for them, and remove their three poisons.

Hu feng miren yu jin xian dao, er yu zhi yan: Duo zai! Nanzi, wei he shi gu, er ru ci lu? You he yishu, neng zhi zhu du?: 'Duo' is the opening sound of the mouth; seeing a person in dire straits, one calls out loudly to rouse him. 'Zai' is an ending particle. This is a metaphor asking: what power do sentient beings have to stop the three poisons and afflictions, that they dare linger in the five turbidities without thinking of escape?

Shi miren hu wen shi yu, fang zhi xian dao, jibian tuibu, qiu chu ci lu: the lost man, on suddenly hearing these words, only then knows it is a dangerous path, and at once steps back, seeking to leave this road. A metaphor for sentient beings who, hearing the bodhisattva's teaching, only then know the danger of the five turbidities and the terror of the three poisons, and at once turn the light inward to seek a way out of the sea of suffering.

Shi shan zhishi, tixie jie shou, yin chu xian dao, mian zhu edu, zhiyu hao dao, ling de anle: this good friend, leading him by the hand, brings him out of the dangerous path, spares him all the evil poisons, and brings him to the good road, giving him peace and joy. A metaphor for the great being's compassionate reception, causing sentient beings to still their delusion and return to the true, to raise right mindfulness, to practise with effort the transcendental holy path, to cut off the seeds of the three poisons, no longer to fall into the three evil destinies, and to attain final peace and joy.

Er yu zhi yan: Duo zai! Miren, zi jin yihou, wu lv shi dao, ci lu ru zhe, zu nan de chu, fu sun xingming: he tells the lost man that if he enters this road he will not only have difficulty leaving but will also lose his life. A metaphor for sentient beings who enter the five desires and six sense-objects, depending on them to create karma, with difficulty in escaping suffering, and moreover harming the life of the Dharma body.

Linbie zhi shi, zhishi you yan: it is a metaphor for a bodhisattva saving one person from suffering and accomplishing the holy path, whereupon that person returns into the Saha world to counsel and guide sentient beings not to do evil again, and so to fulfil the great being's original vow.

Shi gu Dizang pusa ju da cibei, jiuba zuiku zhongsheng, sheng ren tian zhong, ling shou miao le: the good friend is the Bodhisattva Ksitigarbha, and the lost man is the sentient being. The great being, through compassionate transformation, causes them first to be born among humans and gods, and then to cultivate the transcendental Dharma and attain wonderful bliss.

Ruo ye jie zhong, yong chu diyu, wu jietuo shi: if evil karma is deep and heavy, having committed the five deadly offences and the ten evils, then one abides in hell forever, with little hope of liberation.
Fan Wang, Dishi (Brahma King and Indra): the great Brahma king and the lord of the Trayastrimsa heaven in the realm of desire.

Wo ben yeyuan, zhu Yanfu renming: because of the karma of sentient beings, my office and duty is to manage the lives of the people of Jambudvipa, such matters as birth, death, and rebirth; like a household registrar who only records arrivals and departures, without authority to interfere in a person's comings and goings.

Zi shi zhongsheng bu hui wo yi, zhiling shengsi ju bu de an: alas, worldly people cannot comprehend my intention; they do not cultivate good to increase their merit, but delight in doing evil, so that even though I wish to help I cannot, and due to this evil karma, both in life and death they cannot rest in peace.

Huo yi shengxia, shen wu shahai: on the happy occasion of a newborn, one must strictly avoid killing. Master Lianchi said: 'On a birthday one should not kill. When a person has no child he grieves, and when he has a child he rejoices. But he does not consider that all birds and beasts likewise love their young. To celebrate my child's birth while causing the death of another's child, is this at peace with one's heart?' Wanting our own reunion while causing others' flesh and blood to be separated, making our home a slaughterhouse, the wealthier the more killing, is truly inverted.

Zeng wo li gu (it increases my power): when worldly people cultivate goodness, the power of the good spirits increases; when they do evil, the power of the evil ghosts grows strong. The strength of good and evil ghosts and spirits always increases and decreases in accord with the good and evil karma of sentient beings.

Shi zhu juanshu, dang xu she da gongyang, zhuan du zunjing, nian fo pusa minghao, rushi shan yuan, neng ling wangzhe li zhu edao, zhu mogui shen xi jie tuisan: when the suffering of death presses in upon the dying, relatives should, according to their circumstances and strength, make offerings to the Three Jewels and recite the Buddha's name and the sutras, cultivating all virtuous karma. With such good conditions, aiding the deceased, his right mindfulness remains clear, and relying on the power of the Three Jewels and the guardianship of good spirits, he is separated from the masses of demons and ghosts and passes away peacefully, not falling into evil destinies. (How to care for the dying and how to assist the recitation can be found in The Ferry to the End of Life, or Master Yinguang's Three Essential Matters at the End of Life, and Master Hongyi's The Last Stage of Life, in order to do it properly. Those who cultivate the Pure Land especially must be clear on this, lest they fall. I hope all will widely proclaim this principle, for the benefit of self and others.)

blocks.text: Chapter Nine: Reciting the Names of the Buddhas

inline.s: The Bodhisattva Ksitigarbha, for the benefit of sentient beings, expounds the merit of the names of the Buddhas of the past.

Yan liyi shi (expounding matters of benefit): expounding matters of great benefit for the sentient beings of the future, so that they may dissolve karmic hindrances in the midst of birth-and-death, accomplish supreme virtue, and attain final liberation.

Wubian shen (the body without limits): the Buddha has three bodies, the Dharma body, the retribution body, and the transformation body, all immeasurable and boundless. The Dharma body is the Buddha's true body, pervading the ten directions, hence called the body without limits. The retribution body is the Buddha's body of reward, adorned with merit, immeasurable and boundless, hence called the body without limits. The transformation body manifests in the ten directions, countless hundreds of millions of transformations saving beings, also called the body without limits.

Baoxing (the jewel nature): the Buddha, in the stage of cause, benefiting self and others, perfect in both merit and wisdom, ultimately realizes the pure self-nature, the wonderful nature of true thusness, which cannot be likened to anything; compared to the treasures of the world, the Buddha-nature is supremely noble and precious, like a rare jewel of the world, hence called the jewel nature.

Botoumo sheng (the supreme padma): translated into Chinese as the red lotus. The finest among lotus flowers, showing cause and effect at the same time (when a lotus opens it puts forth the seedpod, with the seeds already within; the lotus is the cause and the seeds the fruit, so the lotus reveals cause and effect simultaneously; here 'hua' is the classical character, the same as 'hua' meaning flower), rising unstained from the mud. The Buddha's mind of cause is complete and his virtue of fruit ultimate; dwelling in the defiled world to transform beings, he is not turned by conditions, like the lotus rising from the mud unstained, hence called the supreme padma.

Shizi hou (the lion's roar): a metaphor for the Buddha preaching the Dharma, having attained great fearlessness, able to subdue the deva-maras and the external paths, like the lion's roar that tames all the beasts.
Juliuxun (Krakucchanda): this is Sanskrit for 'what should be cut off.' All afflictions are entirely cut off; it is named from cutting off delusion.
Piposhi (Vipasyin): this means 'pure contemplation,' or 'supreme contemplation,' accomplishing the adornment of ten thousand virtues.
Baosheng (the jewel supremely excellent): named by way of analogy. Having accomplished the fruit of Buddhahood, it is supremely noble, like the most excellent among jewels.

Baoxiang (the jewel characteristics): the Buddha's retribution body has boundless marks of excellence, and the response body is endowed with the thirty-two marks and the eighty minor characteristics. The Buddha's marks of excellence, accomplished by all the virtues, are incomparably sublime and surpass everything.

Jiasa chuang (the banner of the kasaya): 'kasaya' is the Dharma robe of a bhikshu; 'chuang' (banner) has the meaning of high and manifest. Manifesting Buddhahood in the body of the samgha jewel, the fruit of virtue is high and manifest; sentient beings who see it accomplish immeasurable merit. Moreover the holy name is heard in the ten directions, its light shining everywhere, like a banner set high.

Datong shan wang (great penetration, king of mountains): becoming a Buddha, knowing all and penetrating every Dharma, is called great penetration. The king of mountains is a metaphor for the Buddha's fruit of virtue being supremely excellent, as Mount Sumeru rises above the mountains, beyond compare.
Jingyue (the pure moon): having become a Buddha, ultimately pure, with light like the moon.
Shan wang (king of mountains): the meaning is as in 'great penetration, king of mountains.'
Zhisheng (supreme in wisdom): having become a Buddha, possessed of all wisdom, surpassing the sravakas, the pratyekabuddhas, and the bodhisattvas.

Jingming wang (king of pure name): 'wang' (king) means sovereign freedom. The Buddha is the king of the Dharma, free and sovereign over the Dharma. The Buddha's name is supremely excellent, and those who hear it attain purity.
Zhi chengjiu (accomplished wisdom): the Buddha, on first giving rise to the mind, cultivated the ten thousand practices with great wisdom and accomplished them.
Wushang (unsurpassed): the fruit of Buddhahood is supreme and beyond compare.
Miaosheng (the wonderful sound): the Buddha's voice of Dharma is subtle and wonderful; those who hear it never weary.
Manyue (the full moon): the Buddha's merit is complete, like the moon of the fifteenth day.
Yuemian (the moon face): the Buddha's face is like the pure full moon, the fruit of virtue perfectly complete, pure and dignified like the moon.

Ruo you lin mingzhong ren, jiazhong juanshu, naizhi yiren, wei shi bingren gaosheng nian yi fo ming, shi mingzhong ren, chu wu wujian zui, yu yebao deng xi de xiaomie: if there is a person at the point of death, and at least one member of the household recites aloud a single Buddha-name for the sick person, so that it enters the dying person's ear (heard clearly and distinctly), then by this merit, apart from the offenses of the five uninterrupted hells, which are harder to escape, all the rest of his karmic retributions can be eliminated.

(Question: Why did the Bodhisattva Ksitigarbha not mention Amitabha Buddha and urge people to recite Amitabha Buddha? Answer: First, the holy name of Amitabha is commonly seen in the Mahayana scriptures, so there is no need to mention it again. Second, this sutra was spoken in the Trayastrimsa heaven, where the gods are just enjoying their blessings; urging them to be born in the West would make it hard to give rise to faith and vow, while urging them to recite another Buddha and increase heavenly blessings is more readily accepted. As the audience and the circumstances differ, the teaching differs. To hold single-mindedly to the holy name of Amitabha Buddha is also what the Bodhisattva Ksitigarbha delights in and praises.)

blocks.text: Chapter Ten: The Merit of Comparing and Weighing the Conditions of Giving

inline.s: Ksitigarbha asked why the merit of giving differs, and the Buddha answered each separately.
Jiaoliang (to compare and measure): 'jiao' (read jiao); here 'jiao' has the meaning of comparing.

Wo yi shi shi (I have doubts about this matter): the Bodhisattva Ksitigarbha is a bodhisattva of equal enlightenment, and because of his power of vows he did not become a Buddha; how could he not understand the weight of the merit of giving? But for the benefit of sentient beings he asks; moreover the Buddha's teaching must await a question, so the great being expediently brings it about. Furthermore, the merit of giving is inconceivable, and its ultimate, subtle principle is known only to the Buddha, so he requests instruction.
Gongzi yingban gongyang bushi: to personally prepare the offerings and make reverent offerings.
Dang de san jie wei Dishi shen, shou sheng miao le: for three aeons one will be the lord of Trayastrimsa, enjoying supreme and wonderful bliss.

Ruo neng yi ci bushi fuli, huixiang fajie, shi da guowang deng, yu shi jie zhong, chang wei Da Fan tianwang: if one can take the blessing of this giving and dedicate it to the Dharma realm, sharing it with all sentient beings of the Dharma realm, then such great kings and others, in ten aeons, will be the lord of the first dhyana heaven of the realm of form in life after life.

Huixiang (dedication): 'hui' means to turn back, and 'xiang' means to direct toward; turning back the merit one has cultivated and directing it toward sentient beings or toward adorning the Buddha's Pure Land is called dedication. Dedication can be roughly divided into three kinds: dedicating the cause toward the effect, dedicating self toward others, and dedicating the phenomenal toward the noumenal. First, dedicating the cause toward the effect: the merit cultivated in the stage of cause is dedicated toward the future accomplishment of Buddhahood, that is, dedicated toward supreme bodhi. Second, dedicating self toward others: the merit is turned and directed toward all sentient beings, sharing the benefit. Third, dedicating the phenomenal toward the noumenal, also called dedicating toward true thusness and reality, seeking to realize the principle of the one Dharma realm. Giving is a phenomenal matter, while the true nature of all dharmas is the noumenal substance.
Ta (stupa): a tall, pointed structure, of five to a dozen or more tiers; one that stores the Buddha's relics is called a stupa, while one that does not store relics is called a caitya.
Miao (temple): 'miao' means the likeness; the place where the images of Buddhas and bodhisattvas are enshrined, now referring to a monastery.

Geng neng yu ta miao qian, fa huixiang xin, rushi guowang naiji zhu ren, jin cheng fodao, yi ci guobao wuliang wubian: if one can, before a stupa or temple, give rise to the mind of dedication, planting the seed of the bodhi path, then such kings and all people will ultimately accomplish Buddhahood, and this retribution is immeasurable and boundless. With dedication one will become a Buddha in the future; without dedication one only obtains the body of a king and enjoys worldly blessedness that leaks away, a vast difference indeed.
Jingju tianzhu (lord of the Pure Abode heavens): refers to the king of the Mahesvara heaven in the realm of form.
Liu yu tianzhu (lord of the six heavens of desire): refers to the king of the heaven of enjoying the transformations of others' creations.

Ruo weilai shi zhong, you zhu guowang ji poluomen deng, neng zuo rushi bushi, huo fu wuliang. Geng neng huixiang, bu wen duoshao, bijing chengfo, hekuang Shifan zhuanlun zhi bao: the conclusion about dedication is that no matter how great or small the merit, in the end one becomes a Buddha; without dedication one only obtains the retribution of humans and gods. If one can become a Buddha, how much more the bodies of Indra, Brahma, and the wheel-turning king, which are all the more attainable.

Pu quan zhongsheng dang rushi xue (universally urging sentient beings to learn thus): in conclusion sentient beings are instructed that giving should be dedicated. Dedication is like lighting a candle: one candle leads to a thousand, light intermingles with light, endlessly light; the merit is not reduced but rather increases. Giving must be done with a compassionate heart, a humble heart, and a grateful heart, and only then is the merit great; if one gives with an arrogant and proud mind, the benefit gained is very little.

Bushi yinyuan, qi shi rushi (the conditions of giving are thus): a summary of the preceding text. The merit of giving, compared and weighed, is as described above. Whether the blessing is great or small is reckoned according to the strength of the mind, or according to the object of giving and the kind of field planted: the field of blessing, the field of reverence, the field of gratitude, and the field of compassion.

blocks.text: Chapter Eleven: The Earth Spirit's Protection of the Dharma

inline.s: The earth spirit Firm Ground explains the ten kinds of benefit of enshrining the holy image of the Bodhisattva Ksitigarbha.
Jianlao dishen (the earth spirit Firm Ground): the leader of all earth spirits.

Wo cong xi lai, zhangshi dingli wuliang pusa mohesa, jie shi da bukesiyi shentong zhihui, guangdu zhongsheng: the earth spirit Firm Ground reports to the Buddha that from the past up to now, every great bodhisattva he has seen he has regarded and bowed to with reverence, and every great bodhisattva he has drawn near to has, with inconceivable spiritual power and wisdom, broadly saved sentient beings.

Qi yuan shang you bijing (their vows still have an end): the four great bodhisattvas Manjushri, Samantabhadra, Avalokitesvara, and Maitreya also have great karmic connections with Jambudvipa, but their vows to save beings are limited in time and have an end.
Kan (niche): 'kan' (read kan); a niche is a small closet used to enshrine the images of Buddhas and the tablets of spirits.
